The root canal width (yellow dotted line) was calculated as the percentage of the width of the whole root (blue line) of the maxillary canine teeth halfway between the cementoenamel junction (white dashed line) and apex of the tooth (white arrow). For each specimen, mean root canal width was measured from both maxillary canines. If a maxillary canine tooth was missing, demonstrated signs of endodontic disease, or was fractured below the level of the cementoenamel junction, the other canine tooth was solely measured. No skulls had bilateral compromise of maxillary canine teeth that would have precluded this assessment. In this case, the whole root width was measured as 680 pixels and the root canal width was measured as 236 pixels, resulting in a root canal width of 34.7%.

Measurement diagram of the AP x-rays of the whole spine. Three Cobb angles, including the structural and non-structural curves, were shown. The AV (apical vertebra) was defined as the vertebral body that was most distant from the CSVL (common superior vertebral line). If an intervertebral disc was located at the most distant position, then two apical vertebrae were recorded simultaneously, bringing them into one apical region. AV-1 was defined as the vertebral body adjacent to the AV; AV-2 was defined as the vertebral body adjacent to AV-1; AV+1 was defined as the vertebral body adjacent to the AV; and AV+2 was defined as the vertebral body adjacent to AV+1. The UEV (upward slope) and LEV (lower downward slope) were defined as the vertebrae with the largest inclinations at the head and at the tail of the curve respectively. The difference between AV+1 and AV+2 was recorded as the intersegmental imbalance (ISI).

Lateral plain radiograph showing measured factors. The mean height of the vertebral body was defined as the average of the three area heights of the vertebral body ([a+b+c] / 3). The vertebral height ratio was calculated using the following equation : the vertebral height ratio (%) = mean height of the index level / [(mean height of the upper adjacent body + mean height of the lower adjacent body) / 2] × 100. Segmental kyphotic angle (X) was determined at the intersection of lines drawn at the superior plateau of vertebral body and the inferior plateau of vertebral body. The compression rate is calculated as: (b−a)/b×100, wherein 'a' represents the anterior vertebral height and 'b' represents the posterior vertebral height. Vertebral collapse (%) was measured as follows: [(a + c)/2 b]/ [(a + c)/2] 100. The kyphosis Cobb was measured by using the Cobb method. a = upper vertebral height, b = affected vertebral height, c = lower vertebral height.

Sono-anatomical landmarks and ultrasound guidance technique for QL2 block.(QL2, quadratus lumborum 2; 8th intercostal nerve; PQLB, posterior quadratus lumborum block.) The quadratus lumborum (QL) muscle, including the quadratus lumborum muscles (QLM), can be visualized as echoic structures beneath the skin between spinous processes, and usually contains echogenic fluid at the target anatomy.(QLM, quadratus lumborum muscles.) The quadratus lumborum muscle consists of three distinct layers, including quadratus lumborum muscle aponeurotic fibers, intermuscular septae and quadratus lumborum muscle bellies.(QLB, quadratus lumborum block.) Local anesthetic solution can be seen spreading along fascial planes between skin and subcutaneous fat and between quadratus lumborum muscles.(Fascial plane.) Superficial fascia can be visualized as a hypoechoic layer below skin and above quadratus lumborum muscles.(Echolucency.) Needle tip can be visualized as a hypoechoic structure beneath skin.(Needle tip.) Needle trajectory can be visualized along fascial planes between skin and quadratus lumborum muscles.(Needle trajectory.) The QL2 block is performed via suprainguinal approach, which allows visualization of hypodermal space.(Hypodermal space.) Ultrasound guided technique allows visualization of intra-muscular spread of local anesthetic solution.(Intra-muscular spread)

Inferior vena cava diameter measurement technique.The inferior vena cava should be measured in two-dimensional mode at the subcostal window using the long axis distal to the hepatic vein (arrow), approximately 1 - 3cm from the entrance of the inferior vena cava in the right atrium (A). Measurements near the right atrium entrance or near the diaphragm should be avoided. Its diameter can also be measured in M mode simultaneously with the two-dimensional mode to ensure the perfect alignment of the probe, perpendicular to the long axis of the inferior vena cava. In patients under invasive mechanical ventilation, the diameter of the inferior vena cava at the end of inspiration (maximal diameter) and at the end of expiration (minimum diameter) is measured to calculate the distensibility index. The probe must be kept in a fixed position during the respiratory cycle. Image obtained with a GE Vivid T8 echocardiograph. IVC - inferior vena cava.

The pleural effusion is defined not because of (as shown here) a hypoechogenic tone but by the appearance of the lung line (lower white arrows), which indicates the visceral pleura. The pleural line, which is clearly visible (upper white arrows) indicates here only the parietal pleura. All effusions, anechoic or echoic, can be diagnosed using the lung line. The volume of this effusion can be measured using a simple index. Note the underlying nontranslobar lung consolidation (subpleural, of course) with the shadow of the ribs (shading). The quad sign is characterized by a rough trapezium defined by the pleural line, the shadow of the ribs and the lung line. This is a typical example of (mixed) PLAPS.

The images were acquired using a GE General Electric Multidetector Computed Tomography (MDCT) scanner (Bracco Imaging, GE Healthcare, Horten, Norway). The study was conducted in accordance with the ethical standards of The Veterinary Clinical Center of the University of CoImbo (VCCIC). The protocol was registered at the VCCIC Internal Review Board. The center is the primary center for diagnostic imaging of the VCCIC. The study was conducted on healthy dogs. Only dogs that were clinically healthy at the time of imaging were included. The animals were obtained from the VCCIC animal model program. The dogs were acquired for diagnostic purposes or for image processing purposes. Prior to acquisition, dogs were checked for their vital signs, including heart rate, respiratory rate, body temperature, and blood pressure. After acquisition, animals were checked for vital signs and general status. The image quality was evaluated by placing them on a monitor and assessing them on a scale of 1 to 5, where 5 is best quality and 1 is the lowest quality. The data were analyzed using JView 4.3 (Osirix Medical, Montreal, Canada). The ROIs were manually selected and traced using JView 4.3 (Osirix Medical, Montreal, Canada) to calculate liver volume. The liver volume was calculated by subtracting the volume of the gall bladder, caudate lobe, and hepatic lobe fissure from the total volume. Lateral radiograph of the knee demonstrating measurement of Insall–Salvati ratio (ISR) (A/B). The Insall–Salvati ratio measurement method consists of drawing tangential lines to both tibial plates. One tangent line is perpendicular to the tibial plateau tangent, whereas the other tangent line crosses the articular surface. Then, dividing the length of the line BC (distance between the tibial plateau tangent and the point on the tibial shaft) by the length of AB (distance between the medial tibial plateau tangent and the tibial shaft) we obtain the final value of the ratio. The ratio is expressed as A/B
